Targets the NTT bottleneck (91% of Groth16 prover time) via two CUDA optimizations: async double-buffered pipeline eliminating CPU-GPU transfer overhead, and IADD3-path Montgomery multiplication reducing finite-field instruction latency. L74: # GPIR: Enabling Practical Private Information Retrieval with GPUs
L75: 
L76: 【21†Image: Publication image】
L77: Private information retrieval (PIR) allows private database queries; however, it is hindered by intense server-side computation and memory traffic. Numerous modern lattice-based PIR protocols consist of three phases: ExpandQuery (expanding a query into encrypted indices), RowSel (encrypted row selection), and ColTor (recursive "column tournament" for final selection).
L78: ExpandQuery and ColTor primarily perform number-theoretic transforms (NTTs), whereas RowSel reduces to large-scale independent matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMMs). GPUs are well suited for these tasks when combined with multi-client batching, which is necessary for high throughput.
L79: However, batching fundamentally reshapes the performance bottlenecks: while it amortizes database access costs, it expands working sets beyond the L2 cache capacity, causing divergent memory access behavior and excessive DRAM traffic. We present GPIR, a GPU-accelerated PIR system that rethinks kernel design, data layout, and execution scheduling.
L80: We introduce a stage-aware hybrid execution model that dynamically switches between operation-level kernels, which execute each primitive operation separately, and stage-level kernels, which fuse all operations within a stage into a single kernel to maximize on-chip data reuse. For RowSel, we resolve the mismatch between NTT-driven layouts and tiled GEMMs using a transposed-layout design with fine-grained pipelining.
L81: We further extend GPIR to multi-GPU systems, scaling throughput and database capacity with negligible communication overhead. GPIR achieves up to 297.2x higher throughput than PIRonGPU, the state-of-the-art GPU implementation.

L9: # Title:Accelerating Polynomial Multiplication for Homomorphic Encryption on GPUs
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Kaustubh Shivdikar】, 【6†Gilbert Jonatan】, 【7†Evelio Mora】, 【8†Neal Livesay】, 【9†Rashmi Agrawal】, 【10†Ajay Joshi】, 【11†Jose Abellan】, 【12†John Kim】, 【13†David Kaeli】

L15: 【14†View PDF】 【15†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Homomorphic Encryption (HE) enables users to securely outsource both the storage and computation of sensitive data to untrusted servers. Not only does HE offer an attractive solution for security in cloud systems, but lattice-based HE systems are also believed to be resistant to attacks by quantum computers. However, current HE implementations suffer from prohibitively high latency.
L17: For lattice-based HE to become viable for real-world systems, it is necessary for the key bottlenecks - particularly polynomial multiplication - to be highly efficient.
L18: > In this paper, we present a characterization of GPU-based implementations of polynomial multiplication. We begin with a survey of modular reduction techniques and analyze several variants of the widely-used Barrett modular reduction algorithm. We then propose a modular reduction variant optimized for 64-bit integer words on the GPU, obtaining a 1.8x speedup over the existing comparable implementations.
L19: Next, we explore the following GPU-specific improvements for polynomial multiplication targeted at optimizing latency and throughput: 1) We present a 2D mixed-radix, multi-block implementation of NTT that results in a 1.85x average speedup over the previous state-of-the-art. 2) We explore shared memory optimizations aimed at reducing redundant memory accesses, further improving speedups by 1.2x.
L20: 3) Finally, we fuse the Hadamard product with neighboring stages of the NTT, reducing the twiddle factor memory footprint by 50%. By combining our NTT optimizations, we achieve an overall speedup of 123.13x and 2.37x over the previous state-of-the-art CPU and GPU implementations of NTT kernels, respectively.
